claim: By May 2026, cross-platform messaging interoperability mandated by the DMA has become functionally real, exemplified by Latvian startup BirdyChat being able to message WhatsApp users, something 'technically and legally impossible before the DMA.'
stance_target: DMA is producing structural, not merely cosmetic, changes to gatekeeper ecosystems
scope_conditions: EU messaging interoperability, as of May 2026
quoted_support: A user of BirdyChat, a Latvian start-up, can now send messages to someone on WhatsApp, which was technically and legally impossible before the DMA.

claim: Consumer surveys found up to 66% of frequent users report longer/more-friction digital tasks post-DMA-driven product changes, with some users reporting less relevant search results, which critics attribute directly to compliance-driven redesigns rather than incidental effects.
stance_target: DMA compliance changes are costless/frictionless for consumers, supporting a clean pro-regulation reading
scope_conditions: EU consumers, survey undated within piece, as of May 2026 status report
quoted_support: Consumer surveys show simple digital tasks now require more steps for many, with up to 66 per cent of frequent users noting longer searches and some reporting less relevant results.
numbers: up to 66% of frequent users report increased friction

claim: Apple explicitly delayed the EU launch of iPhone Mirroring, citing DMA-driven regulatory changes required, a concrete instance of the DMA imposing a feature-availability cost on EU consumers.
stance_target: regulatory cost is not limited to fines but includes product/feature-timing costs
quoted_support: Apple said DMA compliance has affected how it rolls out features in the EU. The company delayed the launch of iPhone Mirroring for European users, citing regulatory changes required.

claim: As of May 2026, no fines have been issued specifically for default-choice violations (distinct from the €500M anti-steering fine); the EC closed its browser-choice-screen probe into Apple after usability improvements, and the Commission's first formal DMA review (April 2026) declared the law still 'fit for purpose.'
stance_target: current regulatory-exposure status specific to default/choice-screen obligations versus steering obligations
quoted_support: No fines have been issued specifically for default-choice violations, though the Commission closed a probe into Apple's browser choice screen after the company agreed to improve usability.
